analysis.headline: Frontier AI labs are turning into drug developers and big tech is now paying for biology's raw data, while pharma wires AI scientists into whole pipelines: Pfizer signed Edison's Kosmos agent as money keeps moving to the lab bench and the clinic
analysis.summary: Anthropic's S-1 puts drug discovery at the center of its IPO pitch, it owns Mithril's antibodies and says it now runs two to five preclinical programs; OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio, and Pfizer signed a pipeline-wide deal (terms undisclosed) for Edison Scientific's Kosmos AI scientist. Disclosed bio×AI venture since Oct 22 is about $575M (Pathos $237M, Warp $215M, Hexagon $62M, Opentrons $40M, ALLOX $10.5M, Atlas Bio $10M), Formation Bio raised a $600M fund to in-license clinical drugs, and Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open cell-data coalition. Pharma licensing still pays mostly in milestones: Zealand–Generate ($30M of ~$1.2B), AstraZeneca–insitro ($40M of $1.5B).

themes.title: AI labs move from vendor to drug owner, and AI scientists move into pharma pipelines
themes.detail: Anthropic's S-1 sells drug discovery and lab-running models to public investors; the company owns Mithril's muscular-dystrophy antibodies with candidates planned for 2027, and its drug R&D head now puts its pipeline at two to five preclinical programs. OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio and backs Chai; Anthropic's Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M. Former OpenAI staff founded Warp ($215M) and another is reportedly raising about $200M. Startups are getting the same pipeline-wide access: Pfizer is putting Edison Scientific's Kosmos agent to work on its internal data across oncology, immunology and internal medicine. Isomorphic is in talks at $40B or more.

themes.title: AI moves into trial design, recruitment and clinical assets
themes.detail: In one week Boehringer and Microsoft agreed to test digital patient twins, AstraZeneca and Oracle signed a term sheet for AI trial recruitment, Atlas Bio raised a $10M seed to simulate Phase II trials, and BMS is using Claude to judge trial plans. Formation Bio went further, raising $600M to buy Phase 1–2 drugs and run them through its AI-native development platform, and Pathos's $237M also funds AI-led trials. Upstream of the clinic, AstraZeneca is also testing Tremont AI's toxicology-pathology models to speed preclinical safety reads.

themes.title: Make, test and manufacture: money for the physical layer
themes.detail: Warp ($215M, chemistry robots), Multiply Labs ($75M, robotic biomanufacturing), Opentrons ($40M Series E for AI-driven benchtop robots already in most top-20 pharma labs), Xaira's X-Automate, Rivercell (€22M) and BigHat ($75M Series C, wet lab plus autonomous experimentation behind a Phase 1 ADC) all bet the bottleneck has moved from design to the lab. Danaher is building NVIDIA AI into its instruments for closed-loop experiments, and Anthropic's filing talks about models running lab robots.

themes.title: Scale of data over number of platforms, now with big tech paying for the data layer
themes.detail: Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open virtual-cell data coalition alongside DOE and NIH. Flagship merged three single-platform companies into Etcelera around a 150M-cell foundation model and perturbation data, BioGeometry raised past $100M to pair its design model with a virtual cell model and automated lab, and ALLOX and Rivercell raised seeds to generate their own experimental data. Investors now pay for data at scale rather than another model, and shared public datasets raise the bar for startups selling a proprietary atlas.

movers.direction: From models to owning life-sciences workflows
movers.detail: OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio to put pharma-operations agents into Rosalind and is an investor in Chai, which just widened its GSK deal. It also works with Formation Bio (with Sanofi), which just raised a $600M drug-acquisition fund. Alumni are spinning out bio companies: Kevin Weil's Warp, and Miles Wang reportedly raising about $200M.

movers.direction: From selling Claude to pharma to owning drug programs, now part of its IPO story
movers.detail: Anthropic's S-1 (Oct 26) frames drug discovery and model-run labs as core uses and names Novo Nordisk, BMS, AbbVie and Sanofi as customers. It disclosed buying Mithril Medicine in July (after Coefficient Bio this spring), is taking its rare-disease antibodies toward candidates in 2027, and its drug R&D head now describes two to five active preclinical programs; its Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M.

movers.direction: Into clinical development through pharma partnerships
movers.detail: Microsoft is testing digital patient twins and synthetic control arms with Boehringer Ingelheim, and Oracle signed a term sheet with AstraZeneca to use hospital data and AI for trial recruitment. Cloud vendors are pitching at the trial stage, while Google's Isomorphic stays in discovery.

movers.direction: Scaling capital and buying early access to biology's training data
movers.detail: Isomorphic is in talks to raise more than $2B at a valuation of $40B or more, has a data-access roadmap with Abu Dhabi's health department, and with Google DeepMind and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open cell-data coalition, reportedly with a one-year head start on the data.

movers.direction: In the cap tables and now inside lab instruments
movers.detail: NVentures joined Basecamp's $140M Series C, NVIDIA-backed Iambic raised $150M in its IPO, and Danaher is building NVIDIA computing and BioNeMo models into its lab instruments. NVIDIA rarely leads, but it now spans model companies, public drug developers and lab hardware. It is also supplying compute in kind to Biohub's virtual-cell coalition.

movers.direction: Licensing AI platforms for delivery, and holding equity in AI biologics developers
movers.detail: Lilly signed METiS for AI-designed lipid nanoparticles (low double-digit millions upfront, up to $1.1B) and re-upped in BigHat's $75M Series C alongside Amgen and Merck's fund, adding to its run of AI deals this year.

movers.direction: Spreading AI bets from discovery through preclinical safety to trials, plus manufacturing robots and Gulf trial capacity
movers.detail: AstraZeneca signed insitro for MASH and cardiomyopathy targets, a term sheet with Oracle for AI trial recruitment (starting in Abu Dhabi with M42), a research deal with Tremont AI for AI-read preclinical toxicology, invested in Multiply Labs' $75M round, partners with Pathos on an ER PROTAC and is exploring up to 30 trials in Abu Dhabi by 2030.

movers.direction: Buying equity and access in AI for neurology and trial planning
movers.detail: BMS led Pathos's $237M Series E, with Alzheimer's as the first focus, and is using Anthropic's Claude to assess early trial plans, with wider work planned for 2027.

movers.direction: Renting AI platforms in their core areas rather than building them
movers.detail: Astellas licensed AI Proteins' miniproteins (more than $400M), Zealand hired Generate for obesity proteins ($30M upfront), GSK widened its Chai deal after lab tests, and Boehringer went to Microsoft for trial twins.

movers.direction: Consolidating its own AI platforms instead of funding them separately
movers.detail: Flagship merged Cellarity, Etiome and Empress (together $374M raised) into Etcelera with no new capital disclosed, spun Cellarity's sickle cell drug into its own company, and is lining up a big-pharma alliance for the combined platform.
Lightspeed led Warp's $215M launch and is reportedly in talks to lead Miles Wang's ~$200M round.

movers.direction: Owning the make-and-test layer end to end
movers.detail: Lux is in Warp (automated chemistry), Multiply Labs (robotic manufacturing) and Enveda (AI natural-product discovery, now clinical).

Creandum led Atlas Bio's $10M seed, HV Capital led Rivercell's €22M seed, AVP led WhiteLab's $26M Series B and Asabys led ALLOX's $10.5M seed, so European funds are writing larger early cheques for data-first AI biology.

movers.direction: Positioning for AI-biotech IPOs, late rounds and data partnerships
movers.detail: ARK and Duquesne indicated about 40% of Iambic's IPO, ARK, Janus Henderson and Driehaus took part in Recursion's $200M follow-on, T. Rowe Price and a sovereign fund joined Enveda's Series E, CPP Investments is in Hexagon's Series C, the NATO Innovation Fund joined Basecamp, Abu Dhabi is offering its health data to AI drug companies, and the US Energy Department pledged more than $500M over five years to Biohub's open cell-data effort.

movers.direction: Funding domestic AI protein design at $100M scale
movers.detail: China Life Capital led BioGeometry's Series A+, taking its Series A past $100M, with China Development Venture Capital and the Shanghai biomedical fund alongside; the company targets bispecific antibody INDs in 2027.

movers.direction: Funding AI-run drug development asset by asset, not company by company
movers.detail: Unnamed research foundations, endowments, hospitals and philanthropies committed $600M to Formation Bio's first fund, which buys Phase 1–2 drugs into standalone companies. It is the first time this kind of non-venture money has backed an AI drug developer at this scale.

predictions.call: At least one more OpenAI or DeepMind alumni bio startup announces a $100M+ launch round
predictions.based_on: Warp's $215M, plus Miles Wang's reported ~$200M round in talks

predictions.call: Another frontier AI lab or big tech company announces a new bio acquisition (tooling startup or drug developer), after OpenAI–Orchestra and Anthropic–Mithril
predictions.based_on: OpenAI's Orchestra deal; Anthropic's Mithril and Coefficient Bio buys; Microsoft and Oracle trial partnerships

predictions.call: Isomorphic closes $2B+ near $40B, and late-stage AI-biotech rounds price up after it
predictions.based_on: Bloomberg-reported talks; Pathos's valuation nearly doubling since 2025

predictions.call: Pharma–AI discovery deals keep upfronts below ~5% of headline value
predictions.based_on: Zealand–Generate (~2.5%), AZ–insitro (~3%), Lilly–METiS (low double-digit millions of $1.1B)

predictions.call: A third top-20 pharma announces an AI digital-twin, synthetic-control-arm or trial-recruitment partnership with a tech company, or a startup raises $50M+ for it
predictions.based_on: Boehringer–Microsoft digital twins; AstraZeneca–Oracle recruitment term sheet; Atlas Bio's seed; Formation Bio's $600M fund for AI-run clinical development (adjacent, but not a trial-tech raise)

predictions.call: Another AI-native drug developer files publicly for a US IPO
predictions.based_on: Iambic's $150M IPO priced at the midpoint with insider support; Generate Biomedicines' $400M IPO in February

watchlist: Recursion Q3 results on Nov 2 and REC-4881 (FAP) data on Nov 3, a test of whether the first AI-biotech generation can show clinical value
Anthropic IPO: price range, any disclosure of life-sciences revenue or R&D spend, and whether its two to five preclinical programs get their own risk factors
Isomorphic Labs Series C: final size, lead investor and whether the $40B+ valuation holds
AI-scientist agents in pharma: disclosed terms or a first program credited to Edison's Kosmos at Pfizer, more pipeline-wide signings, and whether Edison raises on the back of it
Clinical-stage AI: Formation Bio's first fund-backed in-licensing deals, first Boehringer–Microsoft twin results, and whether AstraZeneca–Oracle becomes binding
analysis.since_last_run: Quiet Saturday: no new qualifying deal was announced since this morning's brief. One gap from earlier coverage was added: on Oct 7 Biohub expanded its Virtual Biology Initiative to a $1.8B coalition, with Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta putting in $300M together, the US Energy Department more than $500M over five years, and NIH contributing existing datasets (the newly named money is closer to $1.3B). That item now feeds the Alphabet/Isomorphic, NVIDIA and sovereign mover entries and the data-scale theme. Anthropic's drug R&D head also said in an Oct 30 interview that its pipeline holds two to five preclinical programs, which is reflected in the Anthropic entry. No prediction resolved: Isomorphic's round is still in talks and no new AI-lab acquisition, IPO filing or trial-tech partnership landed. Seen but left out: Ortet's $500M launch (Sep 29), which targets clinical, lab and revenue-cycle workflows rather than drug discovery, and AstraZeneca's Modella AI purchase, which dates from January. Recursion's Nov 2–3 readouts are next.

items.amount_label: No new capital disclosed ($374M raised by the three predecessors)
items.round: Merger of Cellarity, Etiome and Empress Therapeutics
items.summary: Flagship folded three of its own portfolio companies, Cellarity, Etiome and Empress Therapeutics, into one AI drug discovery company called Etcelera, run by former Adaptimmune CEO Ad Rawcliffe. It combines more than 30 prediction models, a foundation model trained on about 150 million cells and Flagship's in-house AI unit; no new funding was announced.
items.why_invested: Flagship says most Phase II failures come from not knowing what causes disease, and that pooling the three companies' cell-state, disease-timing and multi-omics data with perturbation data should predict which drugs work before trials. Likely also: three sub-scale platforms are cheaper to fund and easier to partner as one.
items.whats_next: First programs are in myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia, plus immunology and metabolic-fibrotic disease. It keeps Cellarity's 2022 Novo Nordisk MASH deal, and a second alliance with an unnamed big pharma is in the works. Cellarity's oral sickle cell drug moves into a separate asset company. Watch for that pharma deal and any fresh financing.
items.why_it_matters: The biggest venture creator in biotech is consolidating its AI platforms around data scale, a sign that standalone single-platform AI biotechs struggle to raise on their own.

items.summary: Barcelona's ALLOX, a spinout of the Centre for Genomic Regulation, maps allosteric pockets by testing huge numbers of protein mutants at once and is building AI models on that data to find druggable sites on hard targets. It closed a $10.5M seed led by Asabys and named Morten Graugaard as independent chair.
items.why_invested: Likely: Asabys, which also led the pre-seed, is backing a proprietary biophysical dataset that few others have, aimed at protein-protein interactions and transcription factors that standard design tools struggle with.
items.whats_next: Building its AI hotspot models, growing the in-house chemistry team, moving several programs toward small-molecule candidates and signing pharma research partnerships.
items.why_it_matters: Another European seed built on generating its own experimental data first, the same bet as Rivercell and Atlas Bio.

items.summary: Brooklyn-founded Opentrons sells open, low-cost liquid-handling robots (Flex and OT-2) that AI systems can drive to design, run and adjust experiments in a loop. It has more than 11,000 robots in over 80 countries and raised a $40M Series E led by healthcare investor Avego.
items.why_invested: Avego's stated view is that every AI-generated hypothesis still has to be tested at a real bench, so the robots that run those tests become a standard layer for autonomous science, and Opentrons already sits in most top-20 pharma labs. Likely also: the installed base gives a cheap route to selling AI software and data tools on top of hardware already in place.
items.whats_next: Spend on AI-driven experiment execution, faster protocol writing through software and AI, tighter links to other lab instruments, and new regions. Watch for agent or model integrations (e.g. with frontier AI labs) and whether the smaller round, well below its $200M SoftBank-led Series C in 2021, signals a flat or lower valuation.
items.why_it_matters: Lab-robot makers are now pitching themselves as the execution layer for AI scientists, the same bet behind Warp, Multiply Labs and Danaher's NVIDIA tie-up, but from the low-cost, high-volume end of the market.

items.summary: Edison Scientific, the FutureHouse spinout that has raised $70M, will roll out its Edison platform and Kosmos AI-scientist agent across Pfizer's R&D pipeline, starting in oncology, immunology and internal medicine. No financial terms were disclosed.
items.why_invested: Edison's pitch is that Kosmos learns from Pfizer's own record of what has worked and failed in human biology and carries lessons between programs, giving Pfizer a compounding in-house advantage rather than a one-off tool. Likely also: Pfizer wants a pipeline-wide agent deal of its own after rivals signed with Anthropic, OpenAI and others.
items.whats_next: Kosmos will build combined world models from public data and Pfizer's internal data, and Edison is embedding its own scientists and engineers in Pfizer teams. Watch for disclosed terms, a named program or decision credited to Kosmos, more pharma signings after Incyte (May) and Pfizer, and whether Edison raises a larger round on the back of it.
items.why_it_matters: Big pharma is now signing pipeline-wide AI-scientist deals with startups as well as frontier labs, and the value being sold is training on the pharma's private failure data, not the model alone.

items.amount_label: Series A+ (size undisclosed) · Series A total >$100M
items.summary: Beijing's BioGeometry, which builds an all-atom molecule design model (GeoFlow) and a virtual cell model (GeoCell) linked to an automated lab, closed a Series A+ led by China Life Capital that takes its total Series A past $100M. The A+ tranche size was not disclosed.
items.why_invested: Likely: backers are buying a Chinese answer to AlphaFold-style design with reported hit rates near 20% across 20+ targets, plus near-term revenue from synthetic biology products, which lowers the risk versus a pure drug-pipeline bet. The lead is the investment arm of a state-linked insurer.
items.whats_next: Upgrading GeoFlow (V4) and GeoCell, expanding the automated lab, and moving several bispecific antibody programs toward IND filings in 2027; synthetic biology revenue is targeted for 2027. Watch for out-licensing to Western pharma, as other Chinese AI biotechs have done.
items.why_it_matters: Chinese state-linked capital is now writing $100M-scale checks for AI protein design, adding a well-funded competitor pool to the US and UK leaders.

items.summary: Formation Bio, the New York AI-native drug developer that works with Sanofi and OpenAI, closed $600M in commitments for its first fund, the Drug Development Accelerator Fund. The fund will only finance Phase 1 and 2 drugs Formation buys or in-licenses, each held in its own company. No LPs were named.
items.why_invested: Stated: LPs get exposure to single drug programs without funding a whole biotech, and Formation gets cheaper capital, more programs and ways to cash out without selling the parent. Its bet is that the bottleneck is pushing stalled clinical drugs through trials, not finding molecules. Likely: mission-driven LPs (foundations, hospitals) like the focus on neglected diseases with little active development.
items.whats_next: Acquire or license 10 to 15 clinical-stage programs over 3 to 5 years, aiming for major clinical results 2 to 4 years after each deal, then partner them with pharma. Watch for the first fund-backed in-licensing deals, the sellers (pharma reprioritizations, distressed biotechs), and whether its AI actually shortens trials.
items.why_it_matters: A first for the field: an AI drug developer raising a fund-style vehicle from non-venture LPs to buy clinical assets one by one. It is not counted as a venture round, but it moves serious money toward AI-run development rather than discovery.

items.summary: Tremont AI, a Boston spinout from the Mahmood Lab at Mass General Brigham that builds foundation models and agents for reading preclinical toxicology slides, signed a research collaboration with AstraZeneca to build and test AI for faster safety screening in animal studies. No financial terms were disclosed; trade coverage appeared Oct 28–30.
items.why_invested: Tremont's stated case is that pathologists still score huge numbers of tissue images by semi-quantitative judgment that varies between experts, and that toxicology-specific models can make those reads measurable, repeatable and quicker to triage, especially rare findings that general-purpose models miss. Likely for AstraZeneca: a cheap way to speed up the safety step that sits between AI-designed molecules and the clinic, building on its earlier pathology-AI moves such as the Modella acquisition.
items.whats_next: The two will refine and benchmark Tremont's models on real safety-assessment work; no timeline or milestones were given. Watch for published validation results, a move from research collaboration to paid deployment, other pharma or CRO signings, and a disclosed seed round for Tremont, which only came out of stealth in late September.
items.why_it_matters: As AI speeds up design, pharma is starting to pay for AI further down the preclinical chain, where safety reads are a slow manual step.

items.summary: Basel-based Atlas Bio builds virtual patients from human-tissue RNA data and uses them to predict how a drug would perform in a Phase II trial, so sponsors can test trial designs before enrolling anyone. It raised a $10M seed led by Creandum on top of a $2.5M pre-seed.
items.why_invested: Creandum's case is that Atlas can simulate trial outcomes without needing sensitive treatment records, which could save sponsors time and money; the pre-seed backers frame it as tackling the high failure rate of mid-stage trials. The founders come from Google language-model research and self-driving cars, which also appealed to tech-first investors.
items.whats_next: Hiring across science and sales, platform work, and signing enterprise customers. The company says first simulated-trial results are due roughly six weeks after the announcement (around early December); watch for a named pharma customer and any prospective validation against a real trial readout.
items.why_it_matters: Seed money is now chasing the costliest step in drug development, Phase II, rather than discovery alone.

items.area: AI-run antibody drug development / rare disease
items.summary: Anthropic disclosed that in July it bought Mithril Medicine, a one-person, Atlas-backed startup whose founder used Claude to coordinate 11 outside labs and take a bispecific antibody for LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy from idea to mouse data in under 18 months. Terms were not disclosed; Anthropic also published early results from Claude work with BMS, Enveda, Generate, BigHat, Divergence Labs and The Column Group.
items.why_invested: Anthropic frames it as a shift from supplying AI tools to pharma toward developing its own medicines, starting with rare childhood diseases, under a model it calls one scientist running several programs with AI doing the coordination. Likely: owning programs gives it hard case studies of what Claude can and cannot do across the whole pipeline, which helps sell to pharma.
items.whats_next: More than 100 bispecific antibodies are in cell testing; Anthropic aims to pick formal candidates for both diseases in 2027, with first human trials possible in late 2028 (LAMA2-CMD) and 2029 (alpha-dystroglycanopathy). The mouse data is preliminary. BMS plans to widen its Claude trial-planning work in 2027.
items.why_it_matters: A frontier AI lab now owns drug programs itself, so AI labs are becoming possible competitors to the biotechs they sell to, not just vendors.

items.area: Frontier AI lab moving into drug R&D
items.summary: Anthropic filed its S-1 for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. The filing presents drug discovery and disease detection as core uses of its models, describes plans to let future models run lab equipment and robots, and confirms in-house discovery work on neglected diseases following July's Claude Science launch. Pharma customers named include Novo Nordisk, BMS, AbbVie and Sanofi. No price range was set; the New York Times reported a raise of about $100B.
items.why_invested: Not a bio deal in itself. Likely: Anthropic puts science, and drug R&D in particular, at the center of its long-term story to justify a very large valuation. Owning programs such as Mithril's antibodies gives that story concrete assets, and existing pharma contracts show enterprise demand beyond coding.
items.whats_next: Price range and roadshow; any segment disclosure of life-sciences revenue or R&D spend; whether the drug programs carry their own risk factors (the filing already flags that models could act in unintended or autonomous ways). After listing, watch whether public money lets Anthropic buy more biotech assets.
items.why_it_matters: The first frontier lab to file for an IPO is pitching public investors on drug discovery, so bio is now part of the core equity story for AI labs, not a side project.

items.summary: Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft agreed a strategic collaboration to test whether AI-built digital patient twins can model disease progression, simulate trials and support synthetic or hybrid control arms. Work starts in lung health; no financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Boehringer says the aim is fewer patients on placebo, faster evidence and better-designed trials, while keeping regulatory and safety standards intact. Likely: Microsoft gains a flagship pharma use case for its cloud and AI stack, building on Boehringer's large Copilot rollout.
items.whats_next: A feasibility phase of modelling and prototyping in lung disease, then possible expansion to other therapy areas, animal health and infrastructure work. No timeline was disclosed; watch for a first hybrid control arm and any regulator engagement.
items.why_it_matters: Big pharma and big tech are taking AI past discovery and into the design of the trials themselves, where most of the money is spent.

items.summary: Xaira unveiled X-Automate: lab workcells, a low-cost vision-guided robotic arm (X-Bot), and an AI agent (X-Scientist) that runs the experiments. In a week-long test, instrument use went from an estimated 54% on a 9-to-5 human schedule to 97%.
items.why_it_matters: This is the same make-and-test bet as Warp Sciences, from a company that already has a lot of funding. Expect lab automation to become a standard part of AI-biotech pitches.
items.why_invested: Not a deal. Xaira is spending its existing funding on in-house, low-cost robotics instead of buying expensive lab automation.
items.whats_next: A planned self-driving lab with about 100 robot arms and a mobile robot platform (Eve). Long-term reliability is still unproven.

items.summary: Pathos uses its Foundry platform, which draws on a very large oncology data set, to pick cancer drug candidates, identify the patients most likely to respond, and design biomarker-driven trials. The new money funds four drug programs, led by the ADC JSKN016.
items.why_it_matters: A big pharma leading a late-stage round at a $3B valuation signals confidence in AI-first clinical development, not just discovery.
items.why_invested: BMS gets equity plus a working partnership: its first joint focus is Alzheimer's, so the money buys BMS a direct line into Pathos's agent-driven candidate scoring as Pathos moves from oncology into neurology. The round came in below the reported $300M target, but the valuation still nearly doubled from $1.6B in May 2025.
items.whats_next: Neurology expansion built on new datasets from Tempus AI; the BMS Alzheimer's program; pushing the JSKN016 ADC and the AstraZeneca ER PROTAC program forward. Watch for first neurology candidates and any BMS opt-in rights.

items.summary: Hexagon Bio mines microbial genomes with a computational discovery platform to find new cell-killing small molecules. It closed a $62M Series C led by The Column Group to take its first antibody-drug conjugate, HEX-360, into the clinic.
items.why_invested: Stated: HEX-360 pairs a HER2 antibody with a payload that blocks protein production, which the company argues can get around resistance to today's topoisomerase and tubulin payloads; preclinical data at AACR 2026 matched or beat an Enhertu-like comparator. Likely: investors are buying a novel-payload ADC story at a time when ADCs are pharma's hottest licensing category.
items.whats_next: HEX-360 is in IND-enabling studies, with a Phase 1 start guided for the first half of 2027. The money also funds new single and dual payloads. Watch for the IND filing and any pharma ADC partnership.
items.why_it_matters: Computational discovery platforms are increasingly being funded on the strength of one clinical-ready asset, not on the platform itself.

items.area: AI preclinical research / health data access
items.summary: Isomorphic Labs and Abu Dhabi's Department of Health will draw up a 24-month roadmap for AI-enabled preclinical research inside the emirate's secure research data environment.
items.why_it_matters: Gulf states are trading access to population health data for a role in AI drug discovery. That data access is becoming a competitive advantage in its own right.
items.why_invested: Abu Dhabi is trading access to its health data and research environment for a role in AI drug discovery. Isomorphic gets data from populations that are underrepresented in drug research.
items.whats_next: A 24-month preclinical research roadmap. In a parallel agreement, AstraZeneca explores up to 30 trials in Abu Dhabi by 2030, with the first six by end of 2026.

links.title: EnterpriseAM: Abu Dhabi health-data agreements

items.summary: Founded by Kevin Weil, OpenAI's former science lead. Human chemists wearing cameras and sensor gloves train robots that synthesize and test compounds around the clock. The company also wants to bring outsourced molecule synthesis back onshore.
items.why_it_matters: One of the largest debut rounds for a wet-lab automation company. It targets the step where most AI drug-discovery pipelines slow down: making and testing the molecules.
items.why_invested: Two stated reasons. First, drugmakers depend on Chinese contract labs such as WuXi AppTec for molecule optimization, which looks riskier amid US–China tension and data-security worries. Second, frontier AI hasn't transformed experiment-driven chemistry the way it has software, because models need real lab data. Warp produces that data, using robots trained on chemists' movements, in the US. Angels include OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, Brian Armstrong and Reid Hoffman.
items.whats_next: Build a fully automated US lab for drug optimization (not discovery). The team of about 20 has already bought robot arms and AI chips. No timeline was given. Watch for a first pharma customer and the lab's opening.

items.summary: An OpenAI researcher is reportedly raising about $200M for his own drug-discovery startup, with Lightspeed in talks to lead. Reported in coverage of Warp Sciences' launch.
items.why_it_matters: This would be a second OpenAI-alumni bio startup in the same month with a $200M-class launch round, and it would make Lightspeed the go-to lead for that group.
items.why_invested: The reported pattern is backing frontier-lab researchers who move into drug discovery. Founders are getting large launch rounds on pedigree before showing any data.
items.whats_next: Watch for the company name, the round closing and the investors. Its scope compared with Warp (discovery or chemistry) will show whether these founders are competing or splitting the space.

items.summary: AI Proteins will design new miniproteins against targets Astellas picks. Astellas gets exclusive worldwide rights and handles development. The upfront amount was not disclosed, and AI Proteins also gets royalties on sales.
items.why_it_matters: Further pharma validation of computationally designed miniproteins as a class of drugs, an alternative to antibodies.
items.why_invested: Astellas says the deal fits its strategy of building its early pipeline through partnerships and new technology. It gets access to a de novo protein-design platform without buying the company, paying mostly on success.
items.whats_next: AI Proteins designs miniproteins against targets Astellas picks (undisclosed). Astellas takes candidates into development. Watch for disclosed targets or therapeutic area, and whether other pharmas sign similar miniprotein deals.

items.area: AI agents for drug development operations
items.summary: Orchestra builds agents that monitor studies, track development timelines and flag delays for pharma teams. OpenAI is folding its team and technology into Rosalind, its suite for life-sciences researchers.
items.why_it_matters: OpenAI's first biotech acquisition, a sign that frontier labs want to own life-sciences workflows rather than just supply the models.
items.why_invested: OpenAI wants agents that run real pharma workflows (study monitoring, timelines, delay flags) inside Rosalind, its life-sciences suite. Buying Orchestra gets it a team and product that already work in pharma operations, rather than building them from scratch.
items.whats_next: Orchestra's team and technology get folded into Rosalind. Watch for Rosalind pricing or enterprise pharma customers, and more OpenAI tuck-in acquisitions in clinical operations or regulatory tools.

items.summary: AstraZeneca and Oracle signed a non-binding term sheet to use Oracle's cloud, AI tools and de-identified hospital data to find trial patients sooner, spot disease earlier and monitor drug safety. The first project is an uncontrolled-hypertension program in Abu Dhabi with UAE health company M42.
items.why_invested: The stated goal is to cut the slow patient enrollment that makes trials long and costly, pairing Oracle's data and AI with AstraZeneca's trial and regulatory know-how. Likely: Oracle gets a top pharma anchor for its health-data business, and AstraZeneca extends its Abu Dhabi trial push.
items.whats_next: Terms still have to be finalised. More projects are planned in the US, Middle East and Europe across cancer, cardiorenal, respiratory, immunology and rare disease, each after legal, privacy and ethics review.
items.why_it_matters: A second big pharma–big tech trial-AI tie-up in a week (after Boehringer–Microsoft) shows the spending moving to recruitment and trial execution.

items.summary: Hong Kong's METiS, which uses its AiLNP platform to generate and optimise ionizable lipids for lipid nanoparticles, signed a delivery collaboration with Eli Lilly. METiS gets an upfront in the low double-digit millions, up to $1.1B in milestones and single-digit tiered royalties.
items.why_invested: Lilly wants nanoparticles that reach specific tissues and perform better, and METiS argues delivery often decides whether a drug works. Likely: Lilly is buying optionality on delivery for its growing nucleic-acid and genetic-medicine pipeline without building lipid design in-house.
items.whats_next: Lipid discovery and optimisation for undisclosed Lilly programs; no diseases or timelines named. Watch for the first named indication and whether METiS adds more Western pharma partners after Hengrui and Boulevard Bio.
items.why_it_matters: AI deal flow is spreading from designing molecules to designing how they get delivered, and pharma will source that from China-based platforms despite US policy pressure.

items.summary: NVIDIA-backed Iambic, which designs small-molecule cancer drugs with its own AI platform, priced its Nasdaq IPO at $16, the middle of its range, selling 9.375M shares for $150M gross.
items.why_invested: Likely: public investors get a clinical-stage AI drug developer with a Phase 1 asset (IAM1363, a brain-penetrant HER2 inhibitor) and a long list of pharma partners. Existing holders ARK and Duquesne signalled they would take about 40% of the deal, which de-risked the book.
items.whats_next: About $75M goes to mid-stage work on IAM1363, about $15M each to IAM217 (KIF18A) and IAM-C1 (CDK2/4), and about $20M to the AI platform. Watch first public-company results and the IAM1363 Phase 1 readout.
items.why_it_matters: The IPO window is open again for AI-native drugmakers with clinical assets, giving late-stage private rounds a public exit to price against.

items.summary: insitro's Virtual Human platform will take AstraZeneca-chosen targets in MASH and cardiomyopathy to development candidates. AstraZeneca then takes over clinical development and gets worldwide rights. Royalties are single-digit.
items.why_it_matters: A typical shape for an AI-discovery deal: a large headline total, but only about 3% guaranteed upfront.
items.why_invested: AstraZeneca calls target selection one of the most critical R&D decisions and wants AI to find the root-cause biology of disease. It is handing that step to insitro's Virtual Human platform in two cardiometabolic areas with high unmet need.
items.whats_next: insitro takes AstraZeneca-nominated targets to development-candidate stage, and then AstraZeneca runs the clinic. Watch for the first candidate nominations, which would trigger milestones.

items.summary: Recursion sold about 61.5M shares at $3.25 to raise roughly $200M, on the same day Sanofi picked the first development candidate from their AI small-molecule collaboration, an oral drug for inflammatory disease that triggers a $10M milestone. The shares jumped more than 16% on the Sanofi news.
items.why_invested: Likely: specialist holders such as Janus Henderson, ARK and Driehaus bought in on the first pharma-picked candidate from the platform, which adds validation and lifts total Sanofi payments to $144M.
items.whats_next: Recursion says the cash extends its runway into 2029. Sanofi funds the program, with Phase 1 expected in 2027 and more than $300M in further milestones possible. Q3 results on Nov 2 and REC-4881 (FAP) data on Nov 3 come next.
items.why_it_matters: First-generation AI biotechs can still raise from public markets, but at a discount and only when a pharma partner backs a molecule.

items.summary: Danaher, which owns Beckman Coulter, Leica, Cytiva and other lab-instrument businesses, agreed to build NVIDIA computing and AI into its instruments: DGX Spark at the edge, RAPIDS analytics and BioNeMo models, with Cosmos and Omniverse digital twins being explored. A small set of priority instruments comes first. No financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Both sides say the aim is a closed loop in which experiment results train models and models choose the next experiments, which shortens the step from prediction to proof. For NVIDIA it puts its stack inside the installed base of lab hardware. Danaher keeps customers free to use other models, which suggests it wants AI as an instrument feature rather than a lock-in.
items.whats_next: Pilot results on the first instruments, then a decision on rolling out across the portfolio. Watch for named pharma pilot sites and for links to Danaher's own autonomous antibody lab.
items.why_it_matters: The incumbent instrument makers now want the 'AI lab' business that startups such as Lila, Warp and Multiply are raising for, and NVIDIA is supplying both sides.

items.summary: Zealand Pharma hired Generate Biomedicines to design multispecific protein drugs for metabolic disease with its AI platform. Generate gets $30M upfront, up to $35M in early preclinical milestones within a total of nearly $1.2B, plus royalties.
items.why_invested: Zealand has worked mostly with peptides and small molecules and wants proteins that hit several obesity targets at once; it pairs its metabolic know-how with Generate's design engine rather than building one.
items.whats_next: Two initial programs; Generate runs research to lead-candidate selection, then Zealand takes over clinical development. Watch for the first candidate nomination and early milestone payments.
items.why_it_matters: Obesity, the biggest market in pharma, is now pulling in AI protein design, again with about 2.5% of the headline value paid upfront.

items.summary: After testing Chai's models in its own labs, GSK turned an evaluation into a broader collaboration that gives it access to Chai's folding and design models across its pipeline. Terms were not disclosed.
items.why_invested: GSK found binders for every target it tested using Chai designs made without target-specific training, and says Chai's models complement the in-house models it retrains on its own lab data.
items.whats_next: Chai supports discovery across GSK programs. Watch for disclosed terms, the first GSK program credited to Chai, and further big-pharma signings after BMS, Lilly, Novartis and Pfizer.
items.why_it_matters: Pharma is now buying AI design only after a wet-lab bake-off, so model companies with proven hit rates are winning platform deals.

items.summary: Bloomberg reported that the Alphabet spinout is in early talks for new funding at a valuation of at least $40B, with one source saying up to $50B. It follows a $2.1B Series B led by Thrive Capital in May 2026.
items.why_it_matters: If it closes at that level, it resets valuations across AI drug discovery, even though the company has no clinical data yet.
items.why_invested: Investors are buying the AlphaFold lineage plus Alphabet backing. The round would extend Alphabet's push to commercialize that research. Reports gave no clinical milestones to justify the step-up.
items.whats_next: A raise of more than $2B is in early talks, with no lead reported. Watch for the closing size and lead investor, and whether a first clinical program is disclosed alongside it.

items.summary: Paris-based Rivercell came out of stealth with a €22M seed round to generate its own cell-response data and train an AI 'virtual cell' that predicts how human cells react to drugs and genetic changes.
items.why_invested: Stated: the founders argue the field's real gap is data, not models, so the company runs its own wet lab to produce it. Likely: the team (a prior exit to Philips, plus Owkin and Bioptimus alumni) made a large seed for Europe easier to back.
items.whats_next: Scale the in-house data platform, expand the Paris lab and launch the virtual-cell programme. Watch for a first pharma data partnership and model benchmarks.
items.why_it_matters: Virtual-cell models are attracting seed money in Europe, and the pitch is owning proprietary data rather than having a better architecture.

items.summary: Multiply Labs builds enclosed robotic clusters that automate manual steps in making cell and gene therapies, and is moving into antibodies, viral vectors and mRNA. Patrick Soon-Shiong's NantWorks led the $75M Series B, taking total funding past $100M.
items.why_invested: Lingotto, which joined the board, argues biologics manufacturing has fallen behind the science and robotics can make it scale as it did in cars and chips. AstraZeneca's stake is a strategic bet that faster AI-led discovery will otherwise jam up at manufacturing.
items.whats_next: More capacity, a faster product roadmap and bigger engineering, regulatory and commercial teams to move from clinical-stage installations to commercial-scale production. Watch for a commercial-product deployment and further pharma investors.
items.why_it_matters: The 'make' bottleneck now extends past the discovery lab to manufacturing, and pharma is investing directly in robots to clear it.

items.summary: The Zuckerberg-backed Biohub grew its virtual-cell data effort into a $1.8B coalition: Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta put in $300M together, the Energy Department pledged more than $500M over five years, and NIH is contributing existing datasets built on over $500M of past federal spending. The aim is an open, AI-ready store of cell-response data and new measurement tools to train predictive models of biology.
items.why_invested: The partners say no single group can generate enough standardized cell data to build an accurate model of how cells respond to drugs or genetic changes, so they are pooling it. Likely also for the tech companies: early exclusive access to the data (reported at one year before public release) feeds their own biology models, including Isomorphic's drug design engine.
items.whats_next: Watch for the first released datasets, how the one-year commercial head start works in practice, which other companies buy in, and whether DOE's autonomous labs start producing data at scale. Note that the new money named is closer to $1.3B; the rest is prior NIH investment.
items.why_it_matters: Big tech is now paying for the raw data layer of biology, not just models, which raises the bar for startups whose edge is a proprietary cell atlas.

items.summary: Paris-based WhiteLab uses its ALFRED platform to design delivery vehicles for genomic medicines, including AAV capsids that crossed the blood-brain barrier in animal work with the Paris Brain Institute. AVP led a $26M Series B.
items.why_invested: Likely: investors are backing evidence that AI-designed capsids work in living animals, plus the novel sequences that could make for defensible IP; the company pitches better brain delivery for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
items.whats_next: In vivo validation of viral and non-viral delivery (including LNPs) and synthetic promoters, building a portfolio of bio-assets to keep or partner, and expansion to the US, Japan and South Korea. Watch for a first pharma licensing deal.
items.why_it_matters: Delivery is becoming its own AI-design category, alongside the Lilly–METiS deal.

items.summary: BigHat, which pairs machine-learning design with its own wet lab and an agentic data platform for protein drugs, raised a $75M Series C co-led by DFJ Growth and Premji Invest, taking total funding to about $223M. Added late: the round fell inside the tracking window but was missed by earlier runs.
items.why_invested: The company says the money backs both its clinical pipeline and the design-and-test platform behind it. Likely for investors: BigHat now has a drug in patients, so its AI-designed biologics are moving from platform promise to clinical readout, and pharma backers Lilly, Amgen and Merck re-upping signals strategic interest.
items.whats_next: BHB810, a CDH17 antibody-drug conjugate for gastrointestinal cancers, is dosing in Phase 1; BHB299, a CEACAM6 T-cell engager, is finishing preclinical work with human trials planned for 2027. Watch for first Phase 1 data, the BHB299 IND and any pharma licensing of either asset.
items.why_it_matters: Growth investors are now funding AI protein-design companies on the strength of clinical assets, with pharma corporate funds staying in the cap table.

items.summary: Enveda uses AI to find and characterize bioactive molecules from plants and microbes. It has three candidates in human testing, including ENV-294 (now in Phase 2 for eczema and asthma) and ENV-308 (for keeping weight off after stopping GLP-1 drugs).
items.why_it_matters: Crossover investors like T. Rowe Price joining suggests an IPO path for clinical-stage AI biotechs.
items.why_invested: With three candidates in human testing, Enveda is no longer a platform bet. Crossover funds (T. Rowe Price) and a sovereign fund joining usually signal positioning ahead of an IPO.
items.whats_next: Phase 2 for ENV-294 (eczema, asthma); ENV-308 for maintaining weight after GLP-1s; ENV-6949 (TL1A) in IBD. An IPO filing is the likely next financing step.

items.summary: London's Basecamp Research trains its EDEN design models on a proprietary genomic dataset gathered through partnerships in more than 30 countries. S32 led an oversubscribed $140M Series C at an $800M valuation, with NVIDIA and Anthropic's Anthology Fund joining.
items.why_invested: Likely: backers are paying for a proprietary data moat that model companies relying on public sequence databases lack; Anthropic and NVIDIA also gain a showcase for frontier-model and GPU use in biology.
items.whats_next: Training the next EDEN models and pushing toward in vivo cell therapies. Watch for a first pharma partnership tied to EDEN designs.
items.why_it_matters: Anthropic is now on a bio cap table, which puts both leading AI labs into biology investing.

items.why_invested: A small, early bet on predicting drug combinations, a less crowded problem than single-target design.

items.why_it_matters: Clinical-trial AI is drawing specialist biotech investors, not only tech VCs.
items.why_invested: Specialist biotech funds (OrbiMed) are backing a model that shortens oncology trials by reading imaging endpoints earlier, which saves money for every sponsor.
